phrases.english_text: The woods, my dad had 100 acres. My grandma, Nan, Tsutli, her mom was Ann. Usgwati was her husband, it was really theirs. So, they felt sorry for Mom and Dad 'cause they were just renting everywhere, but they didn’t have children then. They felt sorry for him, Usgwati, so they told him they would sell to my dad. “I don’t want the children to be moving all the time ” said Usgwati. When I was born it was Usgwati and Ann, they were living in a house near Bunch, that was where I was born. When I was born, it was wooded where we lived. We had cows and horses and, when I was about ten or eleven, I was always out hunting. All my uncles, my dad’s brothers, were all hunters. They were the ones that taught me to hunt . They were hunting deer all the time. But me, I was always shooting squirrels, when I was by myself. When it was deer season, I followed them, and they taught me. ‘Probably about two years, I followed them. And then I learned how to kill deer by myself. And my mom she loved to go fishing. Then I would go with her to go fishing. We were using Radient Line and caught perches. They were delicious to eat, the perches.

phrases.english_text: The woods, my dad had 100 acres. My grandma, Nan, Tsutli, her mom was Ann. Usgwati was her husband, it was really theirs. So, they felt sorry for Mom and Dad 'cause they were just renting everywhere, but they didn’t have children then. They felt sorry for him, Usgwati, so they told him they would sell to my dad. “I don’t want the children to be moving all the time ” said Usgwati. When I was born it was Usgwati and Ann, they were living in a house near Bunch, that was where I was born. When I was born, it was wooded where we lived. We had cows and horses and, when I was about ten or eleven, I was always out hunting. All my uncles, my dad’s brothers, were all hunters. They were the ones that taught me to hunt . They were hunting deer all the time. But me, I was always shooting squirrels, when I was by myself. When it was deer season, I followed them, and they taught me. ‘Probably about two years, I followed them. And then I learned how to kill deer by myself. And my mom she loved to go fishing. Then I would go with her to go fishing. We were using Radient Line and caught perches. They were delicious to eat, the perches.

phrases.english_text: If I really tell the truth, I don’t know how my dad did it, because there were six of us children. When I had my own kids, I found out how hard my dad worked. And why they wouldn’t let us play. I already knew how to work. And when somebody told me “Do this,” I didn’t argue with them, I went and did it. That’s when I realized what they were doing to me, later on, but I had my own kids. I heard somebody talking to my dad, “I raised my boys, if there were rocks laying around, I made them move them. When they moved them, I made them move them back where they got them,” he said. But he didn’t really do it, but if you really think about it —that’s what they made us do, teaching us to work.

phrases.english_text: Well the old man I was talking about, Galnvda, he made Indian medicine. They would leave him — Mom, Dad, and the children. But I didn’t want to go when they went somewhere, I would stay home and watch TV. I would always talk to the old man, Galnvda, and he would predict what was going to happen. “I’m going to tell you something,” he said, “the way we are living today, we are going to lose our language, ” he told me. I was just a little boy, and I knew that was going to happen, but I didn’t believe it. But I was told this old man knew, he said “You all are going to lose the Cherokee language.” And what he said, it is happening today. And Nan Tsutli, was saying the same thing. “You all are going to go through bad times because you all are going to lose your Cherokee language.” The old ones really knew what was going to happen. Like what is happening today, I think, people are going to get mad at me, but I’m going to say it. We didn’t marry our own kind, I did the same thing, I had white wives, so my own children don’t know how to speak Cherokee because of my wife. And Galnvda was saying, “ How we are living today, marrying white people …” How do you say marry ?

phrases.english_text: Yeah, “You are marrying into white.” That’s why the children are going to lose their Cherokee language. That is what is happening today. I’m not using that as an excuse, but my oldest son, Ugvwiyu is his name, I was teaching him but, “I don’t want to learn ” he told me. I was thinking I had a hard time not speaking English growing up. I didn’t want my children to go through a hard time like I did with English. But today a lot has changed from then to now. What they call modern now, it caught up with us. That’s why kids that speak Cherokee are having a hard time. I know because I have gone through it myself. Modern, I’ll just call it “new things.” All these new things that’s coming out for the children, even the TV. I didn’t really watch TV back then. When I was a boy, we had one, but they wouldn’t let me watch it unless they were sitting there with us. When nine o’clock came we had to go to bed. They wouldn’t let us go past that time, because… If I think about it, why? Even the birds go to bed about that time. I thought, “Why did they give us that time to go to bed so early?” . When I think about it, my dad got up about 4:30 in the morning, I guess that’s why we had to go to bed early. He wanted to sleep. He didn’t want to hear the TV. I guess that’s why they made us go to bed at that time.

phrases.english_text: Yeah, “You are marrying into white.” That’s why the children are going to lose their Cherokee language. That is what is happening today. I’m not using that as an excuse, but my oldest son, Ugvwiyu is his name, I was teaching him but, “I don’t want to learn ” he told me. I was thinking I had a hard time not speaking English growing up. I didn’t want my children to go through a hard time like I did with English. But today a lot has changed from then to now. What they call modern now, it caught up with us. That’s why kids that speak Cherokee are having a hard time. I know because I have gone through it myself. Modern, I’ll just call it “new things.” All these new things that’s coming out for the children, even the TV. I didn’t really watch TV back then. When I was a boy, we had one, but they wouldn’t let me watch it unless they were sitting there with us. When nine o’clock came we had to go to bed. They wouldn’t let us go past that time, because… If I think about it, why? Even the birds go to bed about that time. I thought, “Why did they give us that time to go to bed so early?” . When I think about it, my dad got up about 4:30 in the morning, I guess that’s why we had to go to bed early. He wanted to sleep. He didn’t want to hear the TV. I guess that’s why they made us go to bed at that time.

phrases.phonetic_text: stayitv ahti ahseno ahy kehv a
phrases.phonetic_broad: stayitv ati aseno ay kev a
phrases.english_text: Well how I see it, it is going to be difficult for us. Because it’s coming as the older ones predicted already. Also, they say we are going to lose our language, and I believe that is going to happen. And someday the money we are using will not be of any use for us —that’s what the older ones said too. And the gardening —if you don’t know how nothing will grow (famine will happen), even if you don’t know how to hunt, or make a garden. This Walmart that we have today—when Covid-19 happened it was hard on everybody, especially those that don’t know how to cook. McDonald’s wasn’t open, cause some people that’s all they know, they don’t know how to cook. They would go get something to eat and they are the ones that it will be hardest for. They don’t know how to grow things; they just go get something. Also, like the deer— something that’s provided for us, something will happen, so we won’t be able to eat them anymore. So really, we are going to see hard times. Me, I feel sorry for my grandkids. I think about my grandma all the time. She used to scare me. I believe what she said, she was sorry for my kids. I was probably about eight years old; she was crying. I said, “What’s wrong with you? What’s going on?” “It’s going to be hard times, and your kids, and their kids are going to go through a hard time,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going to have kids because I don’t even like girls,” I told her. “You will have kids,” she said. “Cause you’re a man, you will have kids.” I still think about all that they said, my grandpa, my dad’s dad. My grandpa didn’t raise my dad. His aunt was the one that raised him. They took us to Grandpa’s house and my dad knew that they didn’t raise him. After Dad had his kids, they started talking some. That’s where we all gathered, at Grandpa’s house, and that’s what he always said, “It’s going to be difficult.” But I wasn’t listening to what the elders said. When I’m home by myself, I try to remember what they said when they spoke about the future. I wish I had listened, I’d rather have played ball with all my cousins. My grandma used to sit outside—that’s when I began to want to play baseball. I guess I was about five or six years old. I wasn’t playing yet at Sallisaw—that wood my uncle carved (uwelvsv) and the blue jeans that we are wearing today, my grandma used to cut and stuff them, then sewed them up to make balls. That’s what we had for balls. We had two and that’s what we were using playing ball, when somebody hit it too hard it tore up. And my grandma was sitting there. When it broke, she would sew it right back up. And then we started playing again. She had one of them there by her and, when, if this one broke, she would throw that other one in. I guess that’s how much she enjoyed watching us play ball. We always played ball there, and Grandma would sit on the porch watching us and laughing. That’s what I remember the most —that we played well, and because we never had fights. We never went anywhere looking for trouble while we were playing ball. I guess Grandma, she enjoyed that.

And the gardening —if you don’t know how nothing will grow (famine will happen), even if you don’t know how to hunt, or make a garden. This Walmart that we have today—when Covid-19 happened it was hard on everybody, especially those that don’t know how to cook. McDonald’s wasn’t open, cause some people that’s all they know, they don’t know how to cook. They would go get something to eat and they are the ones that it will be hardest for. They don’t know how to grow things; they just go get something. Also, like the deer— something that’s provided for us, something will happen, so we won’t be able to eat them anymore. So really, we are going to see hard times. Me, I feel sorry for my grandkids. I think about my grandma all the time. She used to scare me. I believe what she said, she was sorry for my kids. I was probably about eight years old; she was crying. I said, “What’s wrong with you? What’s going on?” “It’s going to be hard times, and your kids, and their kids are going to go through a hard time,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going to have kids because I don’t even like girls,” I told her. “You will have kids,” she said. “Cause you’re a man, you will have kids.” I still think about all that they said, my grandpa, my dad’s dad. My grandpa didn’t raise my dad. His aunt was the one that raised him. They took us to Grandpa’s house and my dad knew that they didn’t raise him. After Dad had his kids, they started talking some. That’s where we all gathered, at Grandpa’s house, and that’s what he always said, “It’s going to be difficult.” But I wasn’t listening to what the elders said. When I’m home by myself, I try to remember what they said when they spoke about the future. I wish I had listened, I’d rather have played ball with all my cousins. My grandma used to sit outside—that’s when I began to want to play baseball. I guess I was about five or six years old. I wasn’t playing yet at Sallisaw—that wood my uncle carved (uwelvsv) and the blue jeans that we are wearing today, my grandma used to cut and stuff them, then sewed them up to make balls. That’s what we had for balls. We had two and that’s what we were using playing ball, when somebody hit it too hard it tore up. And my grandma was sitting there. When it broke, she would sew it right back up. And then we started playing again. She had one of them there by her and, when, if this one broke, she would throw that other one in. I guess that’s how much she enjoyed watching us play ball. We always played ball there, and Grandma would sit on the porch watching us and laughing. That’s what I remember the most —that we played well, and because we never had fights. We never went anywhere looking for trouble while we were playing ball. I guess Grandma, she enjoyed that.

So really, we are going to see hard times. Me, I feel sorry for my grandkids. I think about my grandma all the time. She used to scare me. I believe what she said, she was sorry for my kids. I was probably about eight years old; she was crying. I said, “What’s wrong with you? What’s going on?” “It’s going to be hard times, and your kids, and their kids are going to go through a hard time,” she said. “I don’t think I’m going to have kids because I don’t even like girls,” I told her. “You will have kids,” she said. “Cause you’re a man, you will have kids.” I still think about all that they said, my grandpa, my dad’s dad. My grandpa didn’t raise my dad. His aunt was the one that raised him. They took us to Grandpa’s house and my dad knew that they didn’t raise him. After Dad had his kids, they started talking some. That’s where we all gathered, at Grandpa’s house, and that’s what he always said, “It’s going to be difficult.” But I wasn’t listening to what the elders said. When I’m home by myself, I try to remember what they said when they spoke about the future. I wish I had listened, I’d rather have played ball with all my cousins. My grandma used to sit outside—that’s when I began to want to play baseball. I guess I was about five or six years old. I wasn’t playing yet at Sallisaw—that wood my uncle carved (uwelvsv) and the blue jeans that we are wearing today, my grandma used to cut and stuff them, then sewed them up to make balls. That’s what we had for balls. We had two and that’s what we were using playing ball, when somebody hit it too hard it tore up. And my grandma was sitting there. When it broke, she would sew it right back up. And then we started playing again. She had one of them there by her and, when, if this one broke, she would throw that other one in. I guess that’s how much she enjoyed watching us play ball. We always played ball there, and Grandma would sit on the porch watching us and laughing. That’s what I remember the most —that we played well, and because we never had fights. We never went anywhere looking for trouble while we were playing ball. I guess Grandma, she enjoyed that.

phrases.english_text: First, I worked at Whirlpool, where they made refrigerators, that’s where I worked. I worked about seven years there and they laid me off. And then I started working at Vian. I was working building dams using big machinery. I’m going to say it in English, “ wastewater” … we fixed the waste water pipes. Then I started working at Sallisaw, at a plant called Borg-Warner. We made water pumps for automobiles, and air filters. I probably worked there about six years. I also got laid off there. And then I started working at Vian. I was working building dams using big machinery. I’m going to say it in English, “ wastewater” … we fixed the waste water pipes. And we were always digging to put in the pipes for water to go through. And I got laid off, then I started at the Casino. I worked there 23 years, and they laid me off, I mean, I quit.
